name: Black Maria

Players desperately avoid winning tricks containing Hearts (1 penalty point each) and especially the dreaded Queen of Spades, 'Black Maria' herself, worth 13 penalty points. history.origins: Developed in Britain in the late 19th century. The game is named after Black Maria, slang for a police paddy wagonâ€”suggesting the Queen of Spades is as much trouble as getting arrested.
timeline: 1880s: Emerges in Britain as a derivative of Hearts-type games.
1900s: Widely played as a family game across Britain and the Commonwealth.
Present: Superseded in global popularity by the American Hearts rules, but still distinctly played in the UK.
history.cultural: A quintessentially British parlor game, often played at Christmas and family gatherings.
history.evolution: The key differences from standard Hearts: Ace and King of Spades also carry penalties (10 and 7 pts respectively in some variants), and the passing direction differs.

setup.players: 3-7 players. (For 3: remove 2â™£ and 2â™¦. For 4: standard 52 cards.)
setup.dealing: Deal all cards as evenly as possible clockwise.

rules.objective: Avoid capturing penalty cards (all hearts plus the Queen, King, and Ace of Spades) in tricks. The player with the lowest total penalty score when someone reaches the agreed limit (e.g. 100 points) wins the game.
rules.gameplay: 1. Player left of dealer leads to first trick. 2. All players must follow suit if they can. 3. Highest card of led suit wins the trick (no trump). 4. Winner of trick leads the next. 5. Play continues until all cards played.
keyRules: Hearts may not be led until a Heart has been discarded on a trick (or in some versions, never on the first trick).
Player with lowest cumuluative score when someone hits 100 (or agreed limit) wins.

strategy.basic: Pass your 3 worst cards (high Spades and Hearts). Never hold the Queen of Spades without the Ace and King of Spades to protect her.
strategy.intermediate: Void Passing: Pass all cards of one suit to create a voidâ€”then dump high-penalty cards when that suit is led.
strategy.advanced: Shooting the Moon: If you receive a powerful hand (many high Hearts + Qâ™ ), consider going for the moon. This requires ALL 13 Hearts + Qâ™ , which is a massive gamble.
tips: Always know who has the Qâ™ . If you passed it to the right, be prepared.
Never lead Spades unless you hold the Queen and want to get rid of it safely.

synthesis.shortDescription: Britain's Hearts. A classic penalty-avoidance game where every Heart is a tax and the Queen of Spades is a catastrophe. Pass wisely, play low, and pray your neighbor takes her.
